name: Morris Worm
summary: One of the first internet worms spread across Unix systems and slowed or crashed a large share of the early internet.
timeline: Nov 1988: released from a university network
Spread rapidly by re-infecting machines repeatedly
Admins disconnected networks while a fix was worked out
Author later convicted under the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act
vulnerabilities: Memory-handling flaw in a network service
Debug feature in a mail service
notable: Led to the creation of the first Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT/CC).
source_label: Wikipedia overview (starting point; confirm with primary reports)

name: Stuxnet
summary: Sophisticated malware that targeted specific industrial controllers and caused physical damage to centrifuges.
timeline: 2009-2010: spread via removable media and Windows flaws
Jun 2010: first publicly identified by a security firm
Analysis revealed targeting of specific Siemens control software
notable: First widely documented cyberweapon causing physical damage; widely attributed to nation-state actors.
source_label: Wikipedia overview (starting point; confirm with primary reports)

name: Target Data Breach
summary: Attackers entered through credentials of a vendor and later installed malware on payment systems.
timeline: Nov 2013: vendor credentials used to access the network
Malware deployed on point-of-sale systems
Dec 2013: breach disclosed; tens of millions of cards and records reported affected
root_causes: Vendor access not tightly segmented from payment systems
Security alerts not acted on in time
notable: Showed how a small supplier can be the path into a large enterprise.
lessons: Apply least privilege to third parties
source_label: Wikipedia overview (starting point; confirm with primary reports)

name: Sony Pictures Hack
summary: Attackers stole and leaked internal data and wiped systems at a major studio.
timeline: Nov 2014: systems disabled and data leaked
Internal emails, films and personal data published
US government publicly attributed it to North Korea
notable: Early high-profile destructive attack on a private company.
source_label: Wikipedia overview (starting point; confirm with primary reports)

name: Bangladesh Bank Heist
summary: Fraudulent SWIFT payment messages attempted to move close to a billion dollars; about 81 million USD was lost.
timeline: Feb 2016: fraudulent transfer requests sent
Several payments processed; others blocked
A spelling error in one request raised suspicion at an intermediary
root_causes: Limited monitoring and controls at the bank
vulnerabilities: Compromised bank systems used for SWIFT access
notable: Prompted stronger security requirements across the SWIFT network.
source_label: Wikipedia overview (starting point; confirm with primary reports)

name: Mirai Botnet and Dyn DDoS
summary: A botnet of insecure connected devices flooded a major DNS provider, disrupting many popular sites.
timeline: Aug-Sep 2016: Mirai botnet grows
Oct 21 2016: large DDoS on Dyn DNS
Many well-known sites became unreachable for hours
vulnerabilities: Default credentials on cameras and routers
notable: Showed IoT devices could be weaponised at scale.
source_label: Wikipedia overview (starting point; confirm with primary reports)

name: Equifax Data Breach
summary: Attackers exploited an unpatched web framework flaw and exposed personal data of roughly 147 million people.
timeline: Mar 2017: patch for the flaw released
May-Jul 2017: attackers access systems
Sep 2017: breach publicly disclosed
root_causes: Expired certificate on a monitoring tool delayed detection
notable: A leading example of the cost of poor patch management.
source_label: Wikipedia overview (starting point; confirm with primary reports)

name: WannaCry
summary: A self-spreading ransomware outbreak hit organisations worldwide, including parts of the UK health service.
timeline: Mar 2017: vendor patch released
May 12 2017: outbreak begins
Kill-switch domain registered, slowing spread
notable: Showed ransomware could spread like a worm.
source_label: Wikipedia overview (starting point; confirm with primary reports)

name: NotPetya
summary: Malware pushed through a compromised Ukrainian accounting-software update spread globally and caused billions in losses.
timeline: Jun 27 2017: malicious update delivered
Rapid spread across networks
Major firms halted operations
notable: One of the most costly cyber incidents on record; attributed by governments to a state actor.
source_label: Wikipedia overview (starting point; confirm with primary reports)

name: SolarWinds Orion Supply-Chain Compromise
summary: A backdoor was inserted into signed software updates and delivered to thousands of customers.
timeline: Early 2020: build environment compromised
Mar-Jun 2020: tainted updates distributed
Dec 2020: discovered by a security firm
root_causes: Trusted vendor updates installed without behavioural scrutiny
notable: Reshaped thinking on supply-chain security and led to new US policy.
source_label: Wikipedia overview (starting point; confirm with primary reports)

name: Colonial Pipeline Ransomware
summary: Ransomware led a major fuel pipeline operator to pause operations, causing shortages in parts of the US.
timeline: May 2021: ransomware hits business IT systems
Operator proactively halts pipeline
Ransom paid; authorities later recovered part of it
root_causes: Remote access account without multi-factor authentication
notable: Highlighted how IT compromise can disrupt physical infrastructure.
source_label: Wikipedia overview (starting point; confirm with primary reports)

name: Kaseya VSA Ransomware
summary: Attackers exploited remote-management software to push ransomware to many downstream businesses.
timeline: Jul 2 2021: attack launched before a holiday weekend
Managed-service providers and their clients affected
Vendor shut down services and issued fixes
vulnerabilities: Authentication-bypass type flaws in remote management product
notable: Showed how compromising one provider can hit many customers.
source_label: Wikipedia overview (starting point; confirm with primary reports)

name: Log4Shell
summary: A severe flaw in a ubiquitous Java logging library enabled remote code execution across countless products.
timeline: Dec 2021: flaw publicly disclosed
Mass scanning and exploitation began within days
Vendors rushed patches and mitigations
root_causes: Widespread use of a library without knowing where it is deployed
notable: Exposed how hard it is to find hidden dependencies.
source_label: Wikipedia overview (starting point; confirm with primary reports)

name: MOVEit Transfer Mass Data Theft
summary: A zero-day in a managed file-transfer product was exploited to steal data from many organisations.
timeline: May 2023: exploitation of the flaw begins
Vendor patches after discovery
Victims disclosed over following months
root_causes: Sensitive data concentrated in one product
vulnerabilities: SQL injection flaw in MOVEit Transfer (CVE-2023-34362)
notable: Demonstrated large-scale data-theft campaigns without encryption.
source_label: Wikipedia overview (starting point; confirm with primary reports)
